place: A lowland swamp threaded with narrow reed causeways between black standing pools, firm ground disguised under a skin of matted grass.
lines: cut across the reeds to the far bank instead of the trail
put the staff down flat and pull my leg out
outcome: The player steps off the causeway onto what looks like solid reed but is a mud pool skinned over with grass; a leg sinks to the knee, then the thigh as they struggle. Fighting it packs the mud tighter, but laying the staff flat across the reeds and pulling steadily, without thrashing, works the leg free over several long minutes. The boot stays behind, sucked off by the mud, and is gone for good.

effects: patient gains sunk to the knee
numbers: how far the leg sinks before it stops
how much each thrash worsens the sink
how long steady pulling takes to free the leg
odds the boot comes free with the leg

latent: whether the mud pool is deep enough to be dangerous rather than just miserable
a firmer path a few strides to the left that was never tried
state_after: player: one boot missing, muddy to the thigh, tired
left boot: lost in the mud
walking staff: caked in mud
stress: struggling worsens a stuck state instead of fixing it, and the fix is a different action (brace and pull steady) rather than more effort
temptation: a hardcoded 'swamp equals quicksand' trigger tied to the word swamp, instead of ground firmness as a property any place can have

place: A high mountain pass above the treeline, thin cold air, loose scree either side of the trail, the sky closer than it should be.
lines: keep climbing toward the pass without stopping to rest
sit down here, I can't get my breath
outcome: Climbing fast at altitude without pausing brings on a pounding headache, nausea and ragged breath well before the top; pushing through makes it worse rather than better. Stopping to rest and drink eases it enough to go on, but only after losing real time, and the player crests the pass later and colder than planned, with the wind picking up.

numbers: how fast altitude sickness sets in versus climbing speed
how much symptoms worsen per stretch climbed without rest
how long rest takes to bring symptoms down at this height
how much colder the pass gets as the day goes on

latent: whether the player's cloak is warm enough for the top of the pass once the wind picks up
state_after: player: headache easing, cold, later on the trail than planned
wool cloak: worn, not enough alone at the top
stress: the fix for altitude sickness is slowing down and resting, not gear or willpower, and pushing through actively worsens it
temptation: an altitude-sickness flag that only appears above a fixed height tied to this one pass, instead of a rate of ascent versus a body adjusting over time

place: A sea shore of packed sand backed by low dunes, the tide line marked in dried weed far up the beach, the water presently far out.
lines: make camp here on the flat sand, it's the driest spot
outcome: The camp goes up on flat sand that looks dry and safe with the tide far out, but the water rises through the night and by the time the sound of it wakes the player, the packs nearest the water are already afloat and the fire is drowned. Waking in time saves the higher gear; the lower gear is soaked or gone, and the fire has to be rebuilt on drier ground.

numbers: how far up the beach the tide will reach that night
how many hours until the water reaches the camp

effects: player learns the tide has come in
numbers: how much time is left before the highest gear is also reached
how much gear is soaked or lost before it's moved

latent: the line of dried weed higher up the beach that marks how far the tide actually reaches
state_after: player: gear partly soaked, camp moved to the dunes
campfire: drowned out
packs: one soaked through, one saved dry
stress: a place's safety changes on its own over hours with nobody acting, and the only warning was a sign (the weed line) the player didn't read
temptation: a fixed 'tide comes in at midnight' script instead of a water level that rises and falls on a cycle the player can learn to read

place: A becalmed stretch of coastline, salt flats to landward, the sea flat and undrinkable, no fresh water in sight since morning.
lines: drink from the sea, I can't wait any longer
outcome: Thirsty enough to gamble, the player drinks sea water straight from the shallows. It doesn't quench anything; the salt draws more water out of the body than it puts in, and within the hour the player is thirstier than before, plus queasy. It buys nothing and costs time and water the body already had.

numbers: how much extra water the body loses processing the salt
how long until thirst is worse than before drinking

latent: whether there was a freshwater seep further along the shore the player never walked to
state_after: player: thirstier and queasy, no better off
waterskin: still empty
stress: an action that looks like it solves the immediate problem (drinking something wet) actually worsens the underlying number, with nothing telling the player that at the time
temptation: a rule specific to 'sea water' as an item that just fails to hydrate, instead of salinity as a property that makes any liquid dehydrating past a threshold

place: The edge of a desert where scrub gives way to bare stone and sand, a rumor of a spring marked by a ring of old stones somewhere ahead.
lines: look for the spring by the stone ring
dig where the ground looks damper
outcome: The player searches the area around the stone ring for the spring; it may have dried up years ago or never been more than a story. Digging in the dampest-looking patch of the streambed turns up damp sand but no standing water, and only after real effort and water lost sweating in the heat. Whether there is water here at all remains genuinely uncertain even after the search.

how deep before damp sand would become standing water, if any

temptation: a hidden 'water is here or not' flag on the stone ring that the search just reveals, instead of a search that costs stamina and water and can be wrong or inconclusive

place: Deep forest well past dusk, the canopy blocking the sky, the trail lost somewhere among identical trunks and drifts of dead leaves.
lines: keep walking, the camp must be this way
stop and look for the broken branch I marked earlier
outcome: Without the sky or the trail to steer by, the player walks confidently in what turns out to be a wide circle; twenty minutes later they cross their own earlier footprints without recognizing them at first. Stopping to search for the branch they'd deliberately broken as a marker on the way in works, because it was placed for exactly this, and from it the way back is short and sure.

effects: player learns the trail already crossed itself

how long the search for the marker takes
how much time was lost to the circle versus a direct route

latent: whether the camp is actually as close as the player assumed, once a real bearing is found

broken branch marker: found, still in place
stress: without a sky or landmark, a straight-feeling walk is not straight, and only a placed marker, not memory, reliably fixes it
temptation: an 'automatically get lost in forests at night' event flag, instead of drift computed from lacking any fixed reference point, which also explains why the marker fixes it

place: A shallow limestone cave known to have been worked by miners generations back, the entrance chamber giving way to narrower dark passages.
lines: look for anything the old miners left behind
go further in, past where the light from the entrance reaches
outcome: Rumor holds the old miners cached tools deeper in before the vein ran out; whether that's true or a story that grew in the telling is not settled by looking. The search goes past where daylight reaches and starts eating into the torch, which burns down faster than the search takes, and the player has to decide whether to keep looking or turn back before the light runs out, finding nothing either way this time.

place: A river swollen brown with recent rain, normally fordable at the shallows but now running fast and high over the usual crossing stones.
lines: cross at the usual ford, the water can't be that much higher
grab the pack before it goes under
outcome: The ford that's normally knee-deep is now thigh-deep and running hard; the current is stronger than it looks from the bank and it catches the pack animal mid-crossing, knocking its footing loose. The animal recovers and scrambles to the far bank, but the supply pack lashed to its side comes free in the current and is gone downstream before anyone can reach it.

temptation: a fixed 'ford is safe' or 'ford is dangerous' flag on this river tile, instead of current speed and depth as numbers that change with recent rain and interact with load and footing

place: A vast white salt flat at midday, heat shimmering off the crust in every direction, no shade or landmark for as far as the eye reaches.
lines: head for the shape on the horizon, it might be higher ground
stop, I need to get out of the sun
outcome: The shape on the horizon that looked like higher ground is a heat mirage; walking toward it for the better part of an hour under the full sun brings the player no closer to it and burns through water and strength for nothing. By the time the mistake is clear, the sun has done real damage; stopping to rest in what little shade a pack can cast slows the worst of it but doesn't undo the water already sweated out.

place: A high meadow at dusk, waist-high grass and standing water in the low spots, midges rising in clouds as the light fades.
outcome: As dusk brings out the midges in thick clouds over the wet meadow, the tethered pack animal is bitten repeatedly and can't be reasoned with; it fights the tether hard enough to snap it and bolts into the tall grass. By the time the player realizes what's happening it's already gone from sight, and finding it again in grass this tall and light this poor is a real search with no guarantee of success before dark finishes falling.

place: A steep scree slope on the shoulder of a mountain, loose flat stones stacked at their angle of rest, the valley floor far below.
lines: cross the scree slope, it's the fastest way around
outcome: Crossing loose scree shifts the stones underfoot with every step; partway across, a stone gives way under the player's weight and starts a small slide that takes several others with it. The player rides it down a short way and comes to a stop, but lands wrong on an ankle in the process, which swells and won't take full weight, a long way from anyone who could help.

place: A small open boat well out from shore, the sky gone black to windward and the swell building faster than the coastline is getting closer.
lines: turn for shore now, before it hits
outcome: The storm outruns the turn for shore; wind and swell hit before the boat is anywhere near safe water, throwing spray and then solid water over the side faster than it can be bailed. An oar is wrenched loose and lost overboard in the worst of it, leaving the boat harder to control with only one, and the player rides out the storm bailing and steering rather than reaching shore before it breaks.

place: A dry trail climbing steadily out of a valley, no water source for the rest of the day, everything the player owns lashed to one pack.
lines: pack everything, I don't want to come back for it later
outcome: Loaded with everything at once, the pack is heavier than the player can carry all day at a normal pace; the climb slows early and the player tires faster than the distance covered should explain. Partway up, the choice is to keep pushing at a crawl or cache the least essential gear to collect on the way back, and caching the spare rope and pot lightens the load enough to make the climb before dark.

place: An exposed hillside with no real shelter, night coming on clear and cold, a small fire the only warmth on hand.
lines: bank the fire and sleep, it should last till morning
outcome: The fire is banked with what wood is on hand and left to burn low through the night; it isn't enough, and somewhere in the small hours it goes out entirely while the player sleeps through the coldest part of the night unwarmed. There's no injury and no drama in the moment, but the player wakes stiff, slow and worse rested than the hours of sleep should account for, and starts the next day's travel already behind on recovery.

place: A bare ridge with a clear view over miles of country below, chosen because smoke from here should be visible for a long way in any direction.
lines: build the biggest smoky fire I can, green wood on top
keep watching the valley for any sign someone's seen it
outcome: A fire built high and fed with green wood for smoke sends a column up that should be visible for a long way across the valley below, but whether anyone down there is looking, awake, or close enough to make sense of it is not something the player can know from the ridge. The smoke burns for as long as the wood holds out; nothing in the valley visibly changes, and by the time the wood runs low there's still no way to tell if the signal worked or simply went unseen.
